title: Rubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
full_text:

By Nandita Bose and Gram Slattery
Oct 17 (Reuters) - The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter as Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.
Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.
"A lot of you don’t know what my decision is yet, but we’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
The waiver comes just weeks before November’s midterm elections, with Trump under pressure over high energy prices as war with Iran disrupts global oil supplies.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday’s order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
Complicating matters is the Graham Act’s call not only for sanctions on Russia but also for tariffs on goods from countries that import Russian energy supplies. Rubio pointed to India, an important US partner that has diversified its energy supplies but remains heavily dependent on Russian oil.
Friday’s executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Senator Darline Graham, a South Carolina Republican whose late brother Lindsey Graham championed the legislation that bears his name, said she disagreed with Trump’s decision and planned to discuss it with him when he campaigns for her next week.
"Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia," she told reporters on Saturday. "Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia."
DIESEL SUPPLIES
Rubio also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.
Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond.
"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get."
Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

Investing.com -- Artificial intelligence is reshaping pharmaceutical research by accelerating drug discovery and increasing demand for experimental data, potentially benefiting laboratory equipment suppliers, according to Bernstein.
In an October 16 report, Bernstein analysts highlighted findings from a webinar with Tom Fleming, co-founder and former CEO of automated laboratory services provider Arctoris.
Fleming said demand for AI training datasets has expanded beyond venture-backed biotechnology companies to major pharmaceutical groups, which now account for most of Arctoris’s data-generation business, excluding certain partnerships.
In some cases, demand for experimental data has increased tenfold or even 100-fold. However, declining costs per data point could offset the financial benefits of higher volumes.
Laboratory instruments capable of producing complex, high-value data at scale are expected to benefit most.
Fleming identified Revvity’s (NYSE) Opera Phenix high-content imaging platform as a potential beneficiary, noting that Arctoris purchased additional units to meet growing demand.
He also highlighted opportunities for 10x Genomics (NASDAQ), whose technologies generate detailed cellular data.
Meanwhile, Illumina (NASDAQ) could benefit from higher sequencing volumes, although falling prices may limit revenue growth.
AI is also expected to increase overall laboratory reagent consumption rather than reduce it.
Although predictive models could eliminate some routine experiments, the growing number of AI-designed molecules and proteins requires extensive physical testing and validation.
Fleming said the greatest long-term value would come from improving clinical trial success rates rather than simply increasing the number of drug candidates.
However, demonstrating meaningful improvements could take years because clinical development remains lengthy and failure rates are high.
The findings suggest AI adoption could reshape spending across the life sciences industry, favouring suppliers of advanced experimental technologies while creating pricing pressure for more commoditised data-generation services.

Investing.com -- Venezuela expects to attract nearly $76 billion in oil investment over the next five years under new agreements, acting President Delcy Rodriguez said Saturday.
Speaking on national television, Rodriguez said the investment commitments include a bilateral agreement with the U.S. covering 17 oil fields and plans to deploy 250 drilling rigs.
The agreement forms part of a broader package of 61 deals aimed at reviving Venezuela’s energy industry and expanding crude production.
"Major investments are coming," Rodriguez said, adding that the nearly $76 billion in expected spending would benefit both Venezuela and its international partners.
The announcement comes as Venezuela seeks to reopen its energy sector to foreign investment following the removal of President Nicolas Maduro in January.
The country’s efforts to attract international energy companies have received backing from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.
Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves but continues to produce significantly less oil than it did a decade ago.
Years of underinvestment, operational difficulties at state-owned oil company PDVSA and U.S. sanctions have constrained the country’s production capacity.
Rodriguez also highlighted a recovery in oil output in the western state of Zulia, a major oil-producing region.
Production in the state has increased from 70,000 barrels per day to 370,000 barrels per day, she said, although she did not specify the period over which the increase occurred.
The government expects Zulia’s output to reach 400,000 barrels per day by the end of 2026.
The planned investments could support Venezuela’s efforts to restore ageing oil infrastructure, expand drilling activity and increase production capacity.
However, the scale of the projected spending will depend on the implementation of the agreements and the country’s ability to sustain foreign investment.
A sustained recovery in Venezuelan crude production could eventually increase global oil supplies as the country rebuilds its energy industry.

title: 5 big analyst AI moves: Meta gets Street-high PT; Salesforce double upgraded
full_text:
5 big analyst AI moves: Meta gets Street-high PT; Salesforce double upgraded
Investing.com -- Here are the biggest analyst moves in the area of artificial intelligence (AI) for this week.
Truist raises Meta to Street-high $1,000 target on Muse AI agent traction
This week, Truist Securities has raised its price target on Meta Platforms to $1,000 from $763, joining Wells Fargo as the highest on Wall Street, citing early traction for its Muse AI agent.
Analyst Youssef Squali kept a Buy rating and added a Muse contribution to his outer-year estimates, with a base case of $28.5 billion in incremental revenue by 2030. Meta shares have risen 21% since Muse launched on September 8, against a 2% gain for the S&P 500.
"With AI infusing higher performance across ads, wearables and Muse (building non-ad revenues from powering personal superintelligence, Muse for Enterprise/SMBs), we see Meta as an AI winner long-term," Squali wrote.
He expects third-quarter revenue of $63.9 billion, up 25% year-over-year and at the high end of management’s $61-64 billion guidance, with cost per thousand impressions rising by double digits again, helped by adoption of Meta’s Advantage+ automated advertising suite.
"Meta’s growth [is] increasingly driven by monetization and retention rather than net new users, in our view," he said.
Truist forecasts 2027 capex of $190 billion, up 32% year-over-year, against a consensus of $193 billion.
BofA double-upgrades Salesforce to Buy, says AI should "deepen dependence" on enterprise platforms
In another bullish move, Bank of America has double-upgraded Salesforce to Buy from Underperform and raised its price target to $285 from $160, reversing its previous concern that AI would disintermediate the software company.
Analyst Tal Liani said conversations with CIOs and other market participants suggest large enterprises are unlikely to replace platforms that house their business logic, data, workflows and compliance frameworks. "If anything, AI should deepen dependence on these platforms," he wrote, adding that "we believe Salesforce offers one of the most comprehensive approaches to enterprise AI adoption."
Liani outlined a four-layer architecture underpinning the bull case: a data layer that establishes governed context; applications such as Sales Cloud and Service Cloud providing business logic and workflows; the agentic layer led by Agentforce supplying reasoning and orchestration; and Slack and the Anthropic-powered Claudeforce enabling natural-language interaction.
He argued that vibe coding and in-house development may address isolated use cases but fall short in managing enterprise-scale data, governance and workflow complexity.
AI revenues remain small and slower-than-expected adoption is the main near-term risk, though Liani pointed to encouraging signs including strong growth in new deal sizes and accelerating performance at Slack. BofA raised its subscription and support revenue growth forecasts for fiscal 2028 and 2029 to 10.4% and 10.5%.
Barclays downgrades Dell, HPE and NetApp as valuations run ahead of enterprise AI inflection
Barclays has downgraded Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and NetApp to Equal Weight from Overweight, saying valuations have run too far with no meaningful enterprise AI inflection yet in sight.
Analyst Tim Long noted the seven enterprise-exposed stocks in his coverage are up an average of about 140% this year against a 12% gain for the S&P 500, with the group now trading at about 21 times estimated 2027 earnings, well above its five-year average of around 15 times.
Dell shares have climbed well over 200% this year, much of it reflecting how well the company has offset memory cost inflation by raising prices. Long’s model has AI server revenue tripling to $75 billion this fiscal year, with potential upside to his $100 billion estimate for fiscal 2028, though growth should decelerate.
"As a result, we expect a meaningful deceleration in growth over the next two years as memory prices normalize and potentially decline," he wrote. Long still sees upside to earnings estimates but said "the scale of the beats should become much smaller," which may limit further gains.
Barclays cut its Dell target to $574 from $603.
’Best of AI trade may be behind us,’ Barclays says
Separately, Barclays strategist Emmanuel Cau said hot inflation data, renewed Middle East tensions and a sharp selloff in chip stocks are testing the bank’s "narrow path higher" thesis for equities, though he attributes much of the weakness to positioning rather than fundamental deterioration.
"Arguably, developments this week were rather unhelpful," Cau wrote, pointing to hot U.S. CPI and PPI prints reviving tightening concerns, Brent crude hitting fresh highs and a sharp drop in semiconductor stocks. The silver lining is that bond yields have eased, suggesting "bonds can still work as safe havens again."
Cau attributed the chip weakness to three factors: intensifying competition in global memory, which hit Korean stocks hardest; renewed funding and valuation concerns after two Asian data center companies delayed IPOs; and continued scrutiny over whether AI capital spending is translating into meaningful revenue.
He said he is less concerned about the memory competition issue and noted underlying fundamentals remain intact, citing strong demand guidance from ASML and TSMC.
That said, Cau said the AI theme is entering "a more mature phase," with valuations, funding needs and revenue visibility facing greater scrutiny. "It is certainly conceivable that the best of the AI thematic trade may be behind us," he wrote, adding that investors should become "far more selective," favoring companies with proven business models, strong cash flows and reasonable valuations.
Mega-cap tech earnings in the coming weeks will be key, Cau continued, while Europe remains a useful diversifier given its lower AI and semiconductor concentration.
HSBC cuts Adobe to Hold on free open-source clone threat to Creative Cloud
Earlier in the week, HSBC downgraded Adobe to Hold from Buy and cut its price target to $267 from $310, flagging headline risks from a free open-source clone of its Creative Cloud suite.
Stephen Bersey, HSBC’s head of U.S. technology research, pointed to reports that ArtCraft — apparently a firm of just a few people — has released what he believes is an auto-coded free clone of Adobe’s software, including versions of Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and Acrobat, with the firm saying it hopes to reach "100% feature parity" within a month.
Bersey distinguished auto-coding from professional vibe coding, where a human reviews code before it is committed, noting it hands full control to the model with minimal human oversight.
"We see many dangers attached to auto-coding projects from both a security, legal, going concern and maintenance perspective, and see this more impacting ’freemium’ and open source enthusiasts for the time being," he wrote, advising users to avoid the download given that open-source code allows AI to identify hacking exploits.
HSBC cut its revenue estimates by about 1% and adjusted earnings estimates by 1-2%, reflecting the risk that some amateur retail users migrate away. Adobe trades at nine times estimated 2027 adjusted earnings against a sector median of 20.7 times, a discount Bersey said is warranted, having identified Adobe as "a realistic candidate for AI-led disruption."

Investing.com -- India’s food safety regulator has issued notices to Nestle India and Hindustan Unilever over allegedly misleading nutritional and health claims on dietary supplements, as authorities intensify scrutiny of food manufacturers.

The latest notices form part of a broader enforcement campaign targeting misleading food labels, questionable marketing practices and violations of manufacturing and storage standards.

title: China proposes export controls on solar-manufacturing technologies

By Colleen Howe
BEIJING, Oct 18 (Reuters) - China has proposed export controls on 12 technologies used to make solar equipment, citing national security concerns, as part of a broader revision that also covers AI and biotechnology.
The ministry of commerce proposed adding the photovoltaic technologies to China’s export-control list, it said in a statement on Friday, adding that greater oversight is needed because solar technologies are increasingly being used in sensitive areas like aerospace and national defense.
Chinese officials held initial talks with manufacturers about potential curbs on advanced solar-panel manufacturing technologies, Reuters reported in April, a move that could threaten plans by US firms such as Tesla to expand production in the US.
Beijing has also curbed exports of solar-manufacturing technology to India, Reuters has reported. Analysts say China is seeking to preserve its dominance as India tries to build up domestic manufacturing and shake off reliance on China.
Export restrictions aim to "guard against the risks of technologies from running out of control or being improperly disseminated, while safeguarding normal international exchanges and cooperation in science and technology," the ministry said.
Exporters must now register certain overseas technology transfers until the export-control catalogue is formally updated. Public consultation on the proposal will close on November 15.
China would ban technologies including those used to make some thin wafers, perovskite and tandem solar cells, as well as large-scale fluidized-bed polysilicon production technologies.
Perovskite is an emerging technology that offers the potential of increased conversion efficiency. Tandem cells combine perovskite and silicon layers to capture more of the sunlight spectrum.
Fluidized-bed technology for producing polysilicon — a key building block for solar panels — is less expensive and more energy-efficient than the dominant Siemens process.
China would also restrict, but not prohibit, exports of advanced solar cell manufacturing technologies, including TOPCon, HJT and XBC.

title: Rubio heads to Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
full_text:

By Gram Slattery and Simon Lewis
WASHINGTON, Oct 18 (Reuters) - While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio travels on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.
The top US diplomat is scheduled to land in Samarkand on Sunday to meet with leaders from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump’s predecessors.
Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel. Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly last September.
Regional politics aside, the trip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign-policy portfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance.
For instance, Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state. He was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April.
Rubio’s previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland.

By Andrea Shalal and David Lawder
BANGKOK, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Last week’s meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble.
Not for the first time, lower-income countries are being rocked by the spillover from the actions of wealthier nations: rising debt service costs, higher inflation and the risk of falling ever further behind economically thanks to the AI boom.
What they got was the stock advice the global lenders always dish out: to shrink fiscal deficits and accelerate economic reforms to attract more private sector investment.
Kristalina Georgieva, the first IMF chief from a developing nation - Bulgaria - said advanced economies were in fact the worst offenders on budget imbalances. She noted that developing countries’ debt levels had actually fallen in recent years, only for surging bond yields elsewhere to drive up their borrowing costs.
Average debt service payments there had more than doubled from a decade ago to 14% of government revenue, crowding out education, healthcare and other critical areas, she said.
ADVANCED ECONOMIES FOCUSED ON THEIR OWN PROBLEMS
At a panel on Saturday, Georgieva said many issues remained unresolved, especially around AI:
"We are in a place where we have many more questions than we have answers. And my alert to everybody is: Do not fall for the guys that pretend they have the answers. They are tricking you."
Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council think tank, said the meetings had flunked their opportunity to come up with guidance or ways to help.
"It’s hard to talk about the developing world when the advanced economies don’t have their act together and are at risk of a fiscal crisis," he said. "And that’s on top of political situations in many of these countries that makes development aid not a priority at the moment."
Mauricio Cardenas, Colombia’s former finance minister and now a research scholar at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs in New York, said many policymakers were left with a deep sense that "something really bad could happen" but no real roadmap to navigate the future.
"The IMF and World Bank are not particularly well prepared for this new phase. They understand that something is going on, they bring in experts on AI," he said. "But in the end, there’s no kind of specific, concrete advice on how to be prepared for something where you don’t really understand how it’s going to unfold."
The geopolitical tensions that have roiled both institutions since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - complicating concerted action - were also evident in Bangkok when nearly half the delegates at an IMF steering committee walked out when Russia’s finance minister spoke.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport delayed the arrival of the head of that committee, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who had to travel overland to Qatar to catch a flight.
And Bangkok itself was a stark reminder of the challenges facing developing countries, still partly under water after floods in September that caused almost $200 million in damage to Thailand’s industrial sector.
RISING INEQUALITY COULD RAISE COSTS IN LONG TERM
Kate Pickett, a professor at the University of York, urged policymakers to focus on more inclusive growth rather than forcing developing countries into tough structural reforms.
"If inequality increases, if poverty deepens, that will increase their costs in the long term," she said. "It’s not enough to describe an economy as resilient. It’s only resilient for the rich and the privileged.”
Ayhan Kose, deputy chief economist at the World Bank, said the global economy had weathered its biggest energy shock - from the US-Israeli war on Iran - better than expected.
But while a global recession had been avoided, he said growth outlooks in both developing and advanced economies were worse than before.
Growth had already fallen off in half of advanced economies, while in developing countries as a whole, it had slowed significantly to around 3.6% from 4.4%.
“People are really worried because resilience today is not a guarantee for resilience tomorrow," he said. "Now they are worried about what will be the next shock, because every six months, if not every three months, there is a new shock."
While no specific initiatives were announced, he said the World Bank remained focused on helping developing countries prepare for advancements in AI, in part by mobilising more private capital, now at triple the levels of 2022.
Yet it, too, has to contend with sharp drops in official development aid and persistent challenges in attracting foreign investment to developing countries.
“The reality on the ground is the reality on the ground,” he said.

By Yasmeen Abutaleb
Oct 18 (Reuters) - North Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in nearly 20 years, but former Governor Roy Cooper has built a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley by relentlessly focusing on affordability and a blunt promise to “make stuff cost less.”
At campaign stops, Cooper, 69, points to his six-year fight to expand Medicaid through a Republican-controlled legislature as evidence he can work across party lines, while attacking Trump-backed healthcare cuts that he says are hitting North Carolinians hard.
“People should not have to make a choice between going to a doctor and putting food on the table,” Cooper said at a September 26 rally in Raleigh, North Carolina. “This ’Big Beautiful Bill’ that gave tax cuts to billionaires has now driven healthcare premiums up more than double for people.”
The White House says the bill cuts taxes, protects Medicaid for eligible Americans and curbs fraud and abuse.
Cooper’s message appears to be working: His lead stood at 14 points in an October SurveyUSA poll. The top super PAC for Senate Republicans has paused TV advertising in North Carolina less than three weeks before the election and begun shifting campaign dollars to defend seats in states that include Iowa and Kansas.
President Donald Trump will rally in the state on Tuesday for Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair who has never held elected office.
The question for Democrats is whether Cooper’s playbook can help them win Republican and independent voters elsewhere, or whether his success is unique to a popular former governor who has never lost an election in four decades of public service.
While some Democrats in heavily Democratic states have embraced Medicare for All, which would provide government-run health insurance for all Americans, Cooper has focused on expanding existing coverage and lowering costs. He points to his fight to expand Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and campaigns on prescription drug and insurance costs.
’OUR STAR ATHLETE AND NO ONE’S PAYING ANY ATTENTION’
“It’s like he’s our star athlete and no one’s paying any attention,” said Neera Tanden, president of the Center for American Progress, a Democratic-aligned think tank, and former White House adviser to President Joe Biden. “The strength of Roy Cooper’s campaign is that he’s able to attract Democrats and independents, but also even some Republicans because he’s focused on cost, but he also has a record.”
Paul Shumaker, a longtime Republican strategist in North Carolina, attributes Cooper’s success to the fact he was already well-known and that Whatley failed to distinguish himself from Trump.
“Roy Cooper came to the US Senate race with a known brand that has been trusted by a majority of North Carolina voters election after election,” Shumaker said. “Republicans are suffering from a lack of trust on the economy right now and Whatley has failed to reestablish that trust.”
Cooper declined an interview request for this story. The Whatley campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
WINNING OVER INDEPENDENTS
North Carolina’s electorate is unusually independent: 40% of registered voters are unaffiliated with either party, compared with 30% each for Republicans and Democrats. Republicans, however, have dominated the state legislature for more than a decade and redrawn districts to strengthen their grip.
Like other Republican candidates, Whatley must contend with Trump’s record-low approval rating, which now hovers at 32%, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll. That poll also showed registered voters preferring Democrats over Republicans nationally by 44% to 37%. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, with 28% of independent voters still undecided.
Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the US Senate, where Democrats must net four seats in the November 3 midterm elections to control the chamber — an already difficult task that makes Cooper’s North Carolina race especially important.
Cooper’s signature bipartisan achievement did not come easily. It took him six years to persuade the Republican-controlled state legislature to pass an expansion of Medicaid under Obamacare in 2023, extending health insurance to more than 700,000 state residents, according to state health department data. After passage, he called it “an unnecessarily long and agonizing journey.”
Whit Ayres, a Republican pollster, said several moderate Democratic governors in the South could replicate Cooper’s success, including Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear.
“The Roy Coopers of the world are not unique,” Ayres said. “The Republicans nominated someone who’s never been elected to any public office at any level anywhere running against a reasonably moderate, popular governor.”
RUNNING AGAINST HEALTHCARE CUTS
Many of the state’s Medicaid gains are likely to be undone by Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” a sweeping tax and budget bill the Republican-led Congress passed last year that cuts about $1 trillion from Medicaid, the largest cut in the program’s history, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office.
Cooper has used Trump’s signature domestic legislative achievement to paint the president and Republicans as depriving North Carolinians of healthcare in order to give billionaires more tax cuts.
He has also focused on congressional Republicans’ decision to curtail COVID-era Obamacare subsidies last year, causing healthcare premiums on the individual health insurance marketplace to spike and more than 200,000 state residents to drop their coverage, according to health policy research firm KFF.
“Roy Cooper has always polled over Republicans,” said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. “This will be the average election for Roy Cooper.”

Investing.com -- China has proposed export restrictions on 12 solar manufacturing technologies, citing national security concerns, in a move that could affect overseas production plans and reinforce Beijing’s dominance in the global photovoltaic industry.
China’s Ministry of Commerce announced the proposal on Friday as part of a broader revision of its technology export-control catalogue, covering artificial intelligence and biotechnology.
The ministry said tighter oversight was necessary because photovoltaic technologies are increasingly used in sensitive sectors, including aerospace and national defence.
Under the proposed measures, China would prohibit exports of certain technologies used to manufacture thin silicon wafers, perovskite and tandem solar cells, alongside large-scale fluidised-bed polysilicon production systems.
Perovskite technology offers the potential for higher solar conversion efficiency, while tandem cells combine materials to capture a broader spectrum of sunlight.
Fluidised-bed polysilicon production is also more energy-efficient and less expensive than the conventional Siemens process.
Beijing would separately restrict, rather than prohibit, exports of advanced solar cell manufacturing technologies, including TOPCon, heterojunction technology (HJT) and XBC.
The proposed controls could complicate overseas manufacturers’ efforts to expand domestic solar production.
Chinese officials previously discussed potential restrictions with manufacturers, raising concerns about expansion plans by U.S. companies, including Tesla (NASDAQ).
China has also tightened access to solar manufacturing technology for India, which is seeking to develop domestic production and reduce reliance on Chinese suppliers.
The proposal reflects Beijing’s efforts to maintain oversight of strategically important technologies while protecting its position in the global solar supply chain.
The commerce ministry said the measures were intended to prevent the uncontrolled spread or misuse of sensitive technologies while preserving legitimate international cooperation.
Exporters must register certain overseas technology transfers pending the formal revision of the export-control catalogue.
Public consultation on the proposal will close on November 15.
If implemented, the restrictions could increase uncertainty for international solar manufacturers seeking access to Chinese production expertise.

Investing.com -- With the upcoming U.S. mid-term election in focus, UBS has assigned a 50% probability to a Democratic sweep, followed by a 40% probability to a divided Congress and a 10% probability to a status-quo Republican sweep, as President Trump’s negative net approval rating is contributing to a difficult environment for Republican Congressional candidates.
Trump’s net approval rating of -21% in part reflects high gas prices, surging mortgage rates, an unpopular Iran war and broader affordability concerns, the firm noted. As a result, the midterms, which serve as a referendum on the sitting president, is likely to shift the Federal government from unified to divided control.
“Republicans are poised to retain a large number of House seats in strongly Republican districts, but polling points to enough seats moving toward Democrats to make a change in control increasingly likely,” UBS said in a report assessing outcome scenarios ahead of the November 3 election.
The Democrats currently need to gain only three seats in the House of Representatives to win a majority in the 435-member chamber, an outcome UBS believes is achievable despite “mid-decade aggressive redistricting” by both parties. However, the firm notes that the size of the Democrats’ advantage and the split between moderate and progressive members is less certain.
In the Senate meanwhile, the Democrats require a net of four seats to reach a 51-seat majority, since Vice President JD Vance would be the tie-breaker in a 50-50 chamber.
“We expect Democrats to protect all of the seats they currently hold, including the two hotly contested open seats in Michigan and New Hampshire,” UBS said, adding that Carolina appears likely to provide one Republican-held pickup. The party would then need to win three of the Republican-held seats in Alaska, Ohio, Maine, Iowa, Texas and Kansas.
While UBS sees a narrow path to Democrats taking back the Senate, close races as well as Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system could mean that the outcome could remain uncertain for weeks after Election Day.
UBS also expects narrow majorities in the event of a Democratic sweep, which would limit the ability of the party to advance legislation without Republican support, or to overcome the President’s veto.
In either outcome, the administration is likely to use executive authority on trade, immigration and foreign policy, the firm said.
Divided government would lead to a greater risk of shutdowns and debt-limit brinkmanship, even if lawmakers reach bipartisan agreements on defense spending, social programs and housing.
A Republican sweep, meanwhile, would also have narrow majorities so that the Senate’s 60-vote threshold would limit the potential of major new initiatives.

BUCHAREST, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country’s territorial waters on Saturday, the defence ministry said.
Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Sunday the drones were likely latest generation Russian drones, flying at speeds similar to fighter jets.
"The ones from last night were flying at 450 km/h, which leads us to think they were Russian-made Geran-4 drones with a turboprop engine," Miruta said. "This is the first time we’ve shot down drones like these."
The drones were brought down days after two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania’s Black Sea coast, the latest in a series of attacks highlighting risks to commercial shipping on NATO’s eastern flank.
Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine.
NATO member Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Romania started shooting down drones that enter its space earlier this year.
The defence ministry said the two drones entered Romanian waters in the Black Sea on Saturday at 1459 GMT and 1501 GMT, respectively.
"NATO is ready and able to react to any potential threat, 24/7, to safeguard our territory and protect our people," a NATO official told Reuters.
Romania’s Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said the North Atlantic Council will have a meeting on Tuesday to discuss Black Sea defence and deterrence.
The two tankers struck earlier this week were hit by Russian drones, a NATO military source told Reuters. Romanian officials are still searching for seven missing crew members.
At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents occurred outside NATO territorial waters.
In Moldova, on Romania’s northeast border, officials said a new drone had crashed in a northern district, near the border with Ukraine. Officials said there were no casualties or damage and specialists were trying to determine the drone’s origin.
Five drones identified as Russian fell on Moldovan territory in a little more than 17 hours on Thursday and Friday, prompting the foreign ministry to issue a statement denouncing Russian actions.

title: Analysis-Carney’s pipeline push is unlikely to bring back Canada’s oil jobs boom
full_text:
Trump endorses Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu for reelection amid Iran war
By Amanda Stephenson
FORT MCMURRAY, Alberta, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney is betting a new pipeline can help revive the country’s oil industry, boost its production and exports, and reduce its dependence on the United States.
Bringing back jobs will be much harder.
In the Alberta oil hub of Fort McMurray – nicknamed Fort McMoney in its heyday more than a decade ago – the tens of thousands of oil field jobs that powered the last boom are unlikely to return, even if Carney gets his pipeline.
Instead, much of the growth in oil sands output is likely to come from automation and efficiency gains rather than large-scale hiring, according to industry forecasts and nearly a dozen interviews with company officials, workers, politicians and academics.
The pipeline backed by Carney would transport 1 million barrels of crude oil a day to a port on the Pacific coast, expanding export capacity to Asia.
Asked by Reuters what the pipeline would mean for the region’s economy, Carney – a former central banker – cautioned against anticipating a return to the oil-boom days.
"I wouldn’t use the term ’boom’," Carney said during a visit to Fort McMurray this month. "I would use ‘sustained growth’."
MORE OIL, FEWER WORKERS
More oil without many more permanent jobs could leave Carney politically exposed on two fronts: Critics on the left say his efforts to fast-track the project’s regulatory approval risks sacrificing the environment, while those on the right argue the deregulation should deliver faster economic growth, higher salaries and more oil jobs.
Low job growth could also further fuel Alberta’s separatist movement, though a referendum on whether to hold a vote to leave Canada is expected to fail on Monday.
An August labor forecast by industry group Energy Safety Canada projects that oil sands employment will fall by 920 jobs or 4% by 2035, even as production grows 6%.
A spokesperson for Energy Safety Canada told Reuters that a new West Coast pipeline would likely reverse the projected job decline but may not add many permanent jobs because of the “structural trend” of producing more oil with fewer workers.
"Nobody should expect that something that happened 15 years ago will happen the same way today," said Dianna De Sousa, CEO of the Fort McMurray Chamber of Commerce.
A spokesperson for Carney declined to comment on the lackluster projections for job creation from the pipeline, referring questions to the Department of Natural Resources, which did not respond.
FROM BOOM TO BUST TO WILDFIRES
From 2000 to 2014, Canadian and international oil companies spent billions to build out the mega-mines and other facilities required to extract bitumen, the thick oil found in northern Alberta.
Fort McMurray became a place where workers fresh out of high school could earn six-figure salaries, putting new pickups and pricey boats in their driveways.
Fly-in, fly-out workers — some from as far as 5,000 km (3,107 miles) away – packed on-site work camps because the city lacked housing.
Then came the 2015 oil price crash, followed by a devastating wildfire one year later. Investors’ growing focus on environmental, social and governance (ESG) criteria combined with the climate policies of Carney’s predecessor Justin Trudeau deepened the slump.
International oil majors exited. Annual oil sands capital investment fell from a C$35 billion ($24.55 billion) peak in 2014 to C$14.2 billion in 2024, according to Statistics Canada. The last major new oil sands project, Suncor’s Fort Hills, started up in 2018.
Alberta’s oil and gas sector employs 435,000 people today, including temporary and part-time workers, 85,000 fewer than in 2014, according to data from Alberta’s Servus Credit Union. Real disposable income in the province is still 10% below 2014 levels. Housing values have declined sharply.
Stronger oil prices and rising production have brought some signs of recovery, including regional population growth for the first time in a decade. But flights from Calgary and other major cities sometimes arrive nearly empty, and vacant commercial spaces dot downtown.
"Things are not getting better," said Jenny Parsons, who has worked as a truck driver and contractor at oil sands sites since moving from Newfoundland 15 years ago.
She said she was earning barely a dollar more an hour than she was in 2011.
WHAT A PIPELINE COULD BRING
No oil sands company has committed the C$100 billion in private investment needed to fill the proposed pipeline and build the carbon capture and storage project Carney has made a condition of federal approval.
Kendall Dilling, head of the Oil Sands Alliance, which represents the five largest companies, said the projects could create thousands of jobs across Canada by the mid-2030s, including upstream investment and supply-chain activity as well as pipeline construction. But many of these jobs would be temporary construction jobs, in British Columbia as well as Alberta, rather than permanent oil-industry jobs.
Some of those jobs no longer exist. Efficiency gains, for example, have cut the time oil companies spend on routine maintenance, which has reduced the number of staff as well as contract positions, he said.
The employment gains “may be less than the absolute peaks that we’ve seen in the past.”
Jason Kenney, Alberta’s conservative premier from 2019 to 2022, cut corporate taxes to get oil sands companies to spend on big projects. But even after oil prices rose and revenue stabilized, companies prioritized shareholder returns over job growth, he told Reuters.
"I was certainly frustrated with them,” he told Reuters. He said he urged companies to allocate some of the tax cut savings to their capital plans.
"The people need to see a benefit, not just the shareholder in New York."
The industry group representing oil companies did not respond directly to Kenney’s comments but said the pipeline provided an opportunity to increase production, create jobs and grow government revenue.
CARNEY FACES RISKS FROM LEFT AND RIGHT
By backing a new pipeline, Carney — who grew up in Alberta’s capital of Edmonton — has brokered an uneasy truce between the federal government and Alberta conservatives. But he has angered some in his own Liberal party by embracing oil to help the Canadian economy survive President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
He has repealed many of Trudeau’s environmental policies, cut the tax rate on new capital investment, and is promoting Canadian oil to investors abroad.
While Carney’s approval rating was at 62% in a September poll from Angus Reid, public sentiment on energy and the environment can shift quickly.
"It’s important to remember that the environmental policies of Justin Trudeau were widely popular at the time," said Lori Williams, a political science professor at Calgary’s Mount Royal University. "If we see more environmentally friendly options starting to come on in the future then I think additional pipelines in Canada will be much harder to sell."
Fort McMurray’s boom had its downsides. The flood of workers strained local infrastructure and created tensions between locals and the thousands of people in work camps. Some oil sands companies now hire more locals to reduce their reliance on fly-in workers, a shift that reflects a leaner but steadier industry.
Still, longtime residents like Colin Hartigan, owner of the city’s Coldwell Banker United office, hope that Carney’s ambitions will bring back at least an echo of the old Fort McMurray.
"At some point, there’s going to be another boom," Hartigan said. "Do I think families here want to see that? Not like in the past, that was a little bit crazy. But do we all pray for it? Absolutely."

title: As AI rally wobbles, stock market’s spotlight turns to earnings
full_text:

By Lewis Krauskopf
NEW YORK, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Stumbles in the market-leading AI trade are set to test investor confidence in the rally in the coming week as Wall Street focuses on quarterly results due from key players including Meta Platforms.
AI-linked stocks, central to the bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary, struggled in recent days, with sharp declines in shares of semiconductor companies and tech hardware firms such as Dell Technologies.
Meta, among the hyperscalers spending massively to build AI data centers, highlights the upcoming week of quarterly reports, along with semiconductor firms Lam Research and Texas Instruments and Elon Musk-led companies SpaceX and Tesla.
"It certainly feels like the narrative in the market is a little bit jittery," said Garrett Melson, portfolio strategist with Natixis Investment Managers Solutions. "Clearly there’s a lot of uncertainty around where AI stands right now."
Worries rippled through markets over risks tied to the financing of the AI build-out boom, which has lifted profits for a wide swath of companies and boosted economic growth. Investors were watching developments with CoreWeave, an AI cloud company with about $50 billion in debt. This week, its shares tumbled.
In other recent signs of caution, strategists at Deutsche Bank and RBC Capital Markets separately pulled back on their recommendations of the tech sector. On October 9, Deutsche Bank strategists said the rotation into tech had "run far and the risk-reward no longer looks favorable in the near term."
Dragged down by the swoon in heavyweight tech and AI stocks, the S&P 500 posted its biggest weekly drop since June. But the benchmark index was only about 2% below its record high set this month. Other sectors, which lagged as tech shined last month, posted solid gains on the week, including healthcare and consumer staples.
"This is very much an on-off switch type of market," Melson said. "When AI is working, it sucks all the oxygen out of the room for the rest of the sectors."
META KICKS OFF HYPERSCALER RESULTS
US reporting season heats up next week, with investors counting on robust performance. S&P 500 companies are expected to have increased earnings by more than 30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES.
Massive outlays on AI data centers and infrastructure underpin the profit jump. Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers that combined are expected to increase their capital spending to about $1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs. Investors are eager for signs the companies can show returns on the investments, which would build confidence that the spending is sustainable.
"One of the most important takeaways of earnings season is whether or not the profitability of the hyperscalers can grow faster than the pace of their capex," said Kevin Shea, senior equity analyst at BNY Wealth.
Shares of Meta, whose market capitalization was about $1.8 trillion, have risen in recent weeks as it launched its Muse AI assistant
"With the cost of capital going up, this capex blowout is going to become more expensive, which raises the bar for returns," said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services. "Meta is going to be the first up to try to provide some color around that question."
SEMIS, TESLA, NETFLIX ALSO ON TAP
Chip companies have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the capital spending boom, but the stocks have cooled off. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index has slumped about 12% this month, although it remained up 57% on the year, compared with a roughly 12% year-to-date gain for the S&P 500.
Wednesday’s reports from Lam Research and Texas Instruments could offer broader indications of demand in the semiconductor industry. Lam Research shares are up 54% in 2026, while Texas Instruments stock is up 59%.
Elsewhere, investors will focus on results from Musk-run companies with market values well over $1 trillion: SpaceX — the newly public space company that also has an AI business — and Tesla, another signature stock of the tech-driven bull market.
Streaming company Netflix, consumer products company Procter & Gamble and engine maker GE Aerospace are among other high-profile reports in the coming week.
The rise in Treasury yields and prospects for further rate hikes from the Federal Reserve also remain front-burner issues for stock investors. Hot inflation data this week boosted bets on another rate increase at the Fed’s meeting at the end of October. Futures pricing suggested most investors still expect the US central bank to wait until its meeting in December to raise rates for a second time this year.
"Another strong earnings season should help equities withstand moderately higher rates," analysts at UBS Global Wealth Management said in a note on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence company said 5% of its shares will be committed to the fund, pending stockholder approval. An additional 2% will be added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.

The company said the fund will enable it to pursue public benefit activities including large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations. Anthropic cited labor market impacts from AI as one example, noting it has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue.
When Anthropic was founded, its co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings. The company also operates an equity donation match program for employees, with approximately half of its workforce participating.
Combined with the new fund, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to public benefit purposes, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
Anthropic said it will share more details about the fund’s structure and governance in the coming months, including the valuation milestones that may increase its stake. The company also plans to release a public benefit report on its progress.

By Kevin Yao
BEIJING, Oct 19 (Reuters) - China’s economy likely sped up slightly in the third quarter from a more than three-year low, helped by hot demand for the country’s technological goods and fresh policy support, but further stimulus may be needed to sustain the momentum.
Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as investment in AI-related sectors cools and trade tensions with the European Union escalate.
China’s strategy of redirecting credit and resources from property towards high-tech industries has created a two-speed economy, where strong factory output and exports mask weak consumption and private investment.
Data due on Monday is expected to show gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.4% year-on-year in July-September, quickening from 4.3% in the second quarter - the weakest pace in more than three years, according to a Reuters poll.
The projected growth is below the 4.6% forecast in a Reuters poll in July and would be below the lower end of the official full-year target of 4.5% to 5%.
"While growth remains near the lower end of the government’s target range, recent data suggest economic momentum improved meaningfully toward the end of the quarter, supported by resilient exports, a recovery in manufacturing activity and the initial effects of policy easing," said Zhou Hao, chief economist at Guotai Junan International.
The official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) showed factory activity rose in September, ending two straight months of contraction, while a private manufacturing PMI showed growth in activity hit a five-month high.
On a quarterly basis, the economy is forecast to have expanded 1.1% in the third quarter, accelerating from 0.9% in April-June, the poll showed.
CHINA’S EXPORTS POWER AHEAD
China’s trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass last year’s record surplus of $1.2 trillion and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners.
A deal with the EU to rein in Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments could weigh on the booming auto trade.
GDP data is due on Monday at 0200 GMT. September activity data is expected to show industrial output growth accelerated to 5.5% year-on-year from 5.2% in August, while retail sales growth edged up to 0.6% from 0.4%. Fixed-asset investment in January-September is projected to have fallen 7.3%, versus a 7.2% drop in January-August.
GDP growth is forecast to edge up to 4.5% in the fourth quarter, putting full-year growth at 4.5%, before easing to 4.4% in 2027, according to the poll.
In late September, Beijing rolled out a fresh round of support measures, including targeted interest-rate cuts and mortgage subsidies, after the cabinet pledged stronger action to shore up growth and meet its annual target.
Earlier this month, authorities also allocated 550 billion yuan ($82 billion) in unused government debt quotas to help ease local government financial strains and support infrastructure spending.
"There remains room for further support measures, such as policies to boost employment and incomes and other measures to boost domestic demand," Lynn Song, ING’s chief Greater China economist, said in a note. "Should economic momentum remain subdued into year-end, policymakers may respond with further fiscal stimulus and a broader easing of monetary policy."
China is likely to rely more on fiscal stimulus to spur growth, as faster producer price gains and a pickup in consumer inflation leave the central bank with limited room for high-profile monetary easing.
Analysts polled by Reuters expect the central bank to keep its benchmark lending rates, the loan prime rates, and banks’ reserve requirement ratio unchanged through the first quarter of 2027.
An expected Politburo meeting and the annual Central Economic Work Conference in December could offer fresh clues on Beijing’s policy priorities for next year.

By Leika Kihara
BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - The Bank of Japan is "doing the right thing" by normalising monetary policy and may need to raise interest rates faster if inflation rises more than expected, a senior International Monetary Fund official told Reuters.
Japan must also clarify how it plans to fund its big spending plans and lay out a medium-term fiscal framework to ease market concerns about fiscal risks, said Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department.
"I would say that they are doing the right thing at this point," Srinivasan said on the BOJ’s efforts to lift its policy rate towards levels deemed neutral to the economy.
"If inflation rises faster than expected, you have to start tightening faster because you don’t want inflation expectations to get un-anchored. It’s data dependent," he said in an interview on Friday.
The remarks came ahead of the BOJ’s key policy meeting later this month, when it could keep rates steady but drop hawkish hints that would reinforce dominant market expectations of a December hike.
Inflationary pressures from the Middle East conflict and brisk AI-demand were among key themes discussed by policymakers gathering for this week’s annual IMF meetings in Bangkok.
BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda, who attended the IMF meetings, said on Friday the central bank will focus on anchoring underlying inflation around its 2% target and won’t tolerate any overshoot, stressing anew its resolve to continue raising interest rates.
For Japan, a weak yen adds to factors pushing up inflation by boosting the cost of raw material imports.
Such mounting price pressures prodded the BOJ to raise rates to a 31-year high of 1.25% in September, following a hike in June. Many analysts expect another rate increase by year-end.
Japan also conducted a rare, coordinated intervention with the US on July 31 to prevent the currency’s slide to near 40-year lows from destabilising financial markets.
In staff analysis included in its report on Asia’s economy, the IMF said a big portion of yen moves since mid-2025 had little to do with fundamental factors such as yield differentials, and instead co-moved with speculative positions in yen futures.
"Japan has a deep foreign exchange market, so as a first line of defense, they have allowed the exchange rate to move," Srinivasan said.
"Bottom line, I would say that the Japanese authorities are fully committed to a freely floating exchange rate. I’ve had many discussions with them. So I don’t doubt that at all," he said when asked if the recent yen intervention was justified.
FISCAL FRAMEWORK NEEDED
Rising global bond yields have also drawn attention at this week’s IMF meetings as debt in advanced economies, including Japan, expanded after years of heavy spending.
Markets worry that Japan may add to its already huge debt pile with the administration’s big spending plans and a two-year cut to the consumption tax from April next year.
Srinivasan said Japan has in fact seen fiscal consolidation proceed more than any other G7 country since the pandemic due in part to rising tax revenues.
"Markets are concerned about the fiscal risks because of the uncertainty" on how Japan would pay for the fresh spending and tax-cut plans, he said. "Japan also would benefit from having a medium-term fiscal framework."
